review_text_raw:
I do not recommend this game. Here's why.
First of all - it's boring. It really is. Gameplay-wise it offers just web browsing, reading stuff and clicking. Telltale's games do not offer much in gameplay, but at least you can watch pretty nice visuals and be engaged in the story. Here you just click and browse. Click and browse. And then browse and click a bit more. When I want to read (and I love reading) I read books, not games.
Second thing - visuals. Yes, the game's style and interface are aesthetically pleasing. But... first developers show lack of any effort to make the game rich in gameplay, then do the same with graphics. Yes they use nice colors. Yes the font is elegant. But it's easy to see how it was designed to be made quickly and effortlessly with those simple vectors. Perfect square on plain background is also aesthetically pleasant, but it doesn't show any craftsmanship. And yes, the art style is not crucial for game to be good. But it helps. Especially when game lacks in other areas.
And finally - the story itself. Game puts in you in the shoes of government worker. And it feels like work to play this game. And what kind of work is that? Spying on people and playing a god. Nothing to be proud of. Looks like you're the part of totalitarian machine, aimed at controlling the people. Taken straight from the Orwell's "Year 1984". Which is not necessarily a bad idea, but... the people you spy on are as obnoxious as your job and character you play. So which side developers really take? It looked like whether the game will try to convey I am doing something good, or those terrorist I'm trying to catch are "good" - I will be very, very disappointed. The "progressive vibe" I started to feel was getting on my nerves, as game was not allowing me to take choices I wanted to take. That I felt would be moral. So it's a frustrating experience, before it finally gets so boring you just stop playing.

The "progressive vibe" I started to feel was getting on my nerves, as game was not allowing me to take choices I wanted to take. That I felt would be moral. So it's a frustrating experience, before it finally gets so boring you just stop playing.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I had my eye on Orwell for quite some time. It looked intriguing; the whole concept of 24 hour constant surveillance isn't that far fetched, if at all, as much as many of us want to believe otherwise. It sat in my wishlist for a while, then it popped up in a Humble Bundle. It sat for a while in my library, then the free episode came up, and reminded me that I owned the game. Might as well give a whirl, yeah?

At first I was enthralled. They built a small universe that was only a hop, skip, and step away from the one I'm familiar with (good ol' US of A), and I was immediately taken in. I went through the first episode dutifully following along, reading everything I could get my hands on in the game. I combed through the info and made sure the data I supplied was tip-top. I finished out the first day (level) and felt good. Then the second day started.

It was the same thing, except I had a couple other targets to watch. I felt like I had already exhausted the gameplay. Find highlighted text, decide whether or not you want it, drag to box. Occasionally switch box from one character to another (which really just become pedantic when you end up only dealing with five or so interconnected characters). There's no real risk unless you just mean to do poorly, if its even possible. You can't really miss anything, so you never have to juggle the lives of all your surveillance targets. Their web-entries, conversation over text and "phone calls" (just more text doesn't read like a real conversation), will patiently wait for you while you sift through all of it. It gets to the point where you're just hunting highlighted words, as if Orwell has already solved the case on its own. Overall, the game is a bit of a dissappointment, which I only finished to see how the story unfolds. You get a few choices, but there is little in the way of making you feel like you had an impact unless you really got into the story.

TL:DR: All in all, the game is repetitive and after playing through the first episode, I really couldn't recommend purchasing the second one unless you really want to continue the story. I can tell the game was a labor of love, but it just doesn't offer any truly unique insights into the surveillance state and the ethical considerations that surround it, let alone the gameplay.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I wish there was a "Maybe" rating. This was so solidly middle of the road. A Perfect 2.5/5. This game is a narrative uncovered through a government surveillance system, and we're really taking the good with the bad here. 

The good: The mechanics of the game are interesting, and pay off in a very satisfying way. The visuals are nice and the interface is inoffensive. 

The bad: The character writing is mealymouthed, badly-paced and lacking a fresh core message. The narrative is hung on characters that are one-dimensional. The message is nothing new, but the 1984 But It's Got Facebook appeal could sell it's rhetorical points a lot easier if these characters felt rounder or even spoke in a slightly modern voice. A game where you follow people's daily communications should lead to these characters feeling richer and more developed. But it managed to avoid that altogether in favor of long, trite conversations, and worldbuilding with zero payoff. There were also a few shaky attempts at social commentary? For a game about investigating people for voicing their Alternative Ideologies, it all felt flimsy, like it didn't have enough confidence to have a real point of view. To it's credit, the story itself had some really interesting and surprising turns! But it was all at the end, AND all at once in a truly maddening choice of pacing.

All this is... fine, I suppose, considering these characters' actions and moral codas don't feel meaningfully attached to the larger ethical decision you're ultimately faced with. Instead, I felt like I was reading a 90's screenplay about Post-college Anarchist Mallrats and their One Cool Professor trying to make their mark on the world. Mostly because Orwell takes itself really, painfully seriously.

Overall, worth playing for the moments where the story and gameplay align nicely, but DEFINITELY get it on sale. Full price? Idk. Torrent Hackers instead. It has the same self-important tone and fakey computer-whiz stuff, but at least that had Angelina Jolie in it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game simply did not resonate with me as much as it should have, and I love my privacy. 

I tried out this game because it was on sale on Steam, and I thought this was an interesting game to try out. 

I don't want to write an extensive review because I do not want to give up any more of my time, but this game has (obviously) a limited amount of replay ability. There's only 4 possibly endings, and while I like the ideas that the game was talking about the issues with privacy, I still don't like the game. I typically don't mind reading, but even on the fastest settings it still was to slow to carry on. It felt like the dialogue was dragging even though I understood what the characters in the game were saying.

I didn't really care about the characters. Abraham was cool in a sense where he created this "Thought" activist group and I did want to learn more about what this group does, but I really didn't care for all the other characters.  I just wanted to get the game over with, and it took a confusing amount of time for me to find an ending to the game. 

I'm just glad that i didn't buy the second game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: I haven't played this game in a while and I don't remember much of it, so take this with a grain of salt. The gameplay is pretty moving, reading, and highlighting text, which isn't bad for what the developers are going for. To make it easier than just reading everything, they highlight themselves some key points for you to choose between. I found it hard to stay invested when you're hearing 2nd hand information on most of the characters (aside from chat messages). I'm pretty sure this is inspired by George Orwell's famous book 1984 (hence Orwell), which I recommend more than this. Don't get me wrong, Orwell story has some depth to it. If you like visual novels then it's great for its immersion, and they have some novel ideas with government surveillance, morality, human nature (a bit of a stretch) etc. I'm just a sucker for some good books. Choice is yours; or just don't play/read either.
